chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Muhammad from Ali ibn al-Hasan al-Maythami from Ali ibn Asbat from Dawud ibn Abi Yazid from Abu Ubaydah ibn Bashir al-Kha'thami said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the road-cutter (qati' al-tariq), and I said, 'The people say that the Imam has discretion in his case; he may do whatever he wishes.' He said, 'Not whatever he wishes, but he acts according to their crimes.' He then specified: 'Whoever cuts the road, kills, and takes wealth, his hand and foot are cut off and he is crucified. Whoever cuts the road, kills, but does not take wealth, he is killed. Whoever cuts the road, does not take wealth, and does not kill, he is exiled from the land. The other view is that we say he has discretion if he fights, brandishes weapons, strikes, and takes wealth, even if he does not kill; in that case, his affair is referred to the Imam. This indicates this distinction.'

key_terms.قُطِعَتْ يَدُهُ وَ رِجْلُهُ: Hand and foot are cut off

ai.seo_question: What are the specific punishments for a road-cutter in Shia jurisprudence based on whether they killed or stole?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies that the Imam’s discretion in punishing the *qati' al-tariq* (bandit) is not arbitrary but strictly proportional to the specific combination of killing and theft, distinguishing between crucifixion, execution, or exile. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on precise legal categorization (*takhassus*) over general discretion, ensuring justice aligns with the severity of the crime as narrated by Imam al-Sadiq (AS).
